title: Padres Minor League Catching Coordinator Detained by ICE at El Paso Airport
excerpt: Oswaldo Pirela, a Venezuelan asylum seeker who has worked in professional baseball for over a decade, was taken into custody while returning home from a work assignment with the team's Triple-A affiliate.
body:
• Oswaldo Pirela, 34, the San Diego Padres' minor-league catching coordinator, was detained by ICE at El Paso International Airport early Sunday while traveling home to Arizona.
  • Pirela arrived from Venezuela in 2014, applied for asylum, and is currently pursuing an EB-2 visa. His family says he has continuously maintained valid work authorization.
  • The Padres confirmed the detention but offered no details on its cause. MLB said the team is in contact with Pirela's family.
  • The case is the latest collision between professional baseball and the Trump administration's expanded immigration enforcement operations.

A San Diego Padres minor-league coach is being held in federal immigration custody after being detained at an airport while traveling home from a routine work assignment, the latest case to highlight the reach of the Trump administration's deportation operations into American professional sports.

Oswaldo José Pirela, 34, works as the Padres' minor-league catching coordinator and was in El Paso, Texas, for work connected to the team's Triple-A affiliate, the El Paso Chihuahuas. He was taken into custody by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement at El Paso International Airport early Sunday morning while preparing to return to Arizona, where he lives with his wife and two U.S.-born daughters.

"He is truly an exemplary person. He lives for his family, is a hardworking man, a devoted father and husband, and a man of faith."

— Jorge Pirela, cousin

What Happened at El Paso Airport

ICE agents detained Pirela at approximately 4:00 to 4:30 a.m. Mountain Time on Sunday. Arrest records show he is being held at the El Paso Processing Center and remained there as of Tuesday morning. ICE had not publicly provided a detailed explanation for why he remained in custody.

The Padres confirmed the situation in a statement: "We recently became aware of the detainment of minor league catching coordinator Oswaldo Pirela in El Paso, Texas. We are working to gather additional information and will not have any further comment at this time."

Reports from The Athletic indicated Pirela was not carrying his physical work-permit card when he was detained, though his family insists all his documentation has been consistently maintained through proper legal channels.

A Life Built in American Baseball

Pirela arrived in the United States from Venezuela in 2014 and filed for asylum. His family says he fled political persecution and pursued the asylum process through established legal channels. He is currently going through the EB-2 visa process, a category reserved for professionals with advanced degrees or exceptional ability.

"Since the time he applied for asylum, he has continuously renewed his work authorization whenever it was approaching expiration. Everything has always been done through the proper legal process," Jorge Pirela told CNN.

Pirela has spent much of his adult life in baseball. He played in the Texas Rangers' minor-league system from 2009 to 2011 before transitioning into coaching. He joined the Padres organization in 2024 and now works throughout their player-development system.

His sister, Daniela Pirela, told NBC News: "He did everything lawfully as the U.S. asks. He loves this country."

Baseball and Immigration Enforcement

Pirela's detention is the latest intersection between Major League Baseball and the Trump administration's aggressive deportation policy. Last summer, the Los Angeles Dodgers said they denied ICE entry to their parking lots outside Dodger Stadium as the administration conducted large-scale sweeps for undocumented immigrants in the Los Angeles area. Protesters gathered at the stadium to oppose ICE's presence, and the incident raised alarms across Southern California.

The Padres organization has also previously navigated immigration issues. Earlier this year, top prospect Humberto Cruz pleaded guilty to a charge related to transporting undocumented immigrants and was placed on the minor league restricted list before self-deporting to Mexico.

"He did everything lawfully as the U.S. asks. He loves this country."

— Daniela Pirela, sister

Broader Pattern of Asylum Seeker Detentions

The Trump administration has widened the scope of its immigration enforcement operations, increasingly detaining asylum seekers who have followed legal processes. The administration is looking to increase the speed of deportations and has cast a wider net about who can be arrested, even as many of those caught up in enforcement operations have pending legal cases and valid work authorization.

Pirela's family is seeking legal assistance and waiting for clarity on why a routine work trip ended with him in federal custody. Major League Baseball confirmed the team has been in touch with the family regarding the situation.

The case underscores the uncertainty facing hundreds of thousands of asylum seekers with pending cases across the United States, many of whom have built careers, families, and deep community ties while awaiting resolution of their immigration status.
nri_angle: The detention of a professional baseball coach with valid work authorization illustrates the expanding reach of immigration enforcement that affects all immigrant communities, including South Asians navigating the asylum and visa systems.
